Farmer:
Description: A seasoned vegetable farmer who regards growing crops and feeding consumers as a vocation, closely conntected to nature. I personally experienced that low sales prices and high production cost make it difficult to make a living from farming. I believe spraying crops with Bt is a crucial contribution to control harmful pests and maximize crop yield in a manner that is safe for the farm workers applying the biopesticide, safe for consumers, and environmentally friendly. I believe that farming contributes to preserving the heritage of my country and shapes the world we live in, thus providing attractive environments for both locals and tourists.. Short-term goals: Pest control: To actively control harmful pests by spracing crops with biopesticides to increase yield and minimize pest-related damages to the crops.
Maximization of (high quality) crop yield: To maximize crop yield in a manner that keeps production costs low and is as environmentally friendly and as safe as possible for consumers, workers, and the environment.
Workers’ safety: To ensure that the workers use pesticides without negative effects on their health.
Earn a living: To make a living and provide for my family through farming, which is aided by biopesticide use that increases crop yield in a cost-effective manner.
Education and advocacy: To educate the public on the importance of prudent use of biopesticides in farming in order to feed feed the world at affordable costs, while maintaining cultivated landscapes, conserving the country’s heritage and contributing to its attractiveness for tourism.
. General aim: Ensure the well-being of farmers and farm-workers by devising ways to safely use biopesticides that are accepted by the consumers. . Scientific foundation: Pest control: Scientific research supports spraying crops with Bt as an effective tool for controlling harmful pests and maximize crop 
Maximization of crop yield: Pest control increases the yield of crops in general and also contributes to a higher share of products that are of a quality that is accepted by consumers, thus leading to higher revenues for farmers. 
Workers’ safety: Application of Bt biopesticides has been shown to adhere to high safety standards in terms of workers safety and protection. 
Consumer safety: Bt biopesticides have been used for decades and there is limited evidence of hazardous effects on humans. 
Environmental safety: Compared to chemical pesticides Bt biopesticides are environmentally friendly and there is limited evidence of hazardous effects on biodiversity. . Ethical foundation: Sustainability: Farmers argue that the use of biopesticides is a cornerstone of ecologically sustainable farming and assures that pests can be managed without affecting biodiversity.
Conservation: Farmers argue that farming in a cost-effective manner is enabled by using pesticides, which in turn maintains the cultural heritage and the cultivated landscapes of Central Europe.
Local authority food safety officer:
Description: As a representative of food authorities, my principal function is to protect consumers and raise compliance through partnership, science and food law enforcement. I must ensure that all food businesses meet their legislative obligations and that all food products sold and consumed are correctly labelled and safe to eat.
I believe that a prudent use of Bacillus thuringiensis (e.g Bt) pesticides  in Germany could help to meet the SDG goals and contribute to the green deal. The benefits of using Bacillus thuringiensis biopesticide include its effectiveness in controlling insect pests in various agricultural settings. However, its use must be strictly regulated to ensure consumer safety.
Bt is one of the most important biopesticide in the EU from an ecological ae well as an economic point of view, However, there are indications that its unregulated use poses a health risk to the consumer. Bacillus thuringiensis strains display a similar repertoire of potential virulence genes on the chromosome as B. cereus strains, and these genes can be actively expressed in B. thuringiensis, eventually resulting in food borne illness. Thus, the levels of B. cereus considered a risk for consumers are also likely to be valid for B. thuringiensis, as they cannot be distinguished at the chromosomal level. 
The use of Bt  can also contribute to the reduction of chemical/ synthetical pesticides, which may have harmful effects on human health and the environment. However, Bacillus cereus and B. thuringiensis strains are usually not discriminated in clinical diagnostics or food microbiology, so the actual contribution of the two species to diseases is unknown.
. Short-term goals: Safety Assessment and Monitoring: As food authority we aim to ensure the safety of biopesticides containing Bacillus thuringiensis by conducting thorough safety assessments, including the identification of genetic determinants for toxins and regular monitoring of strains used as biopesticides to differentiate them in outbreak situations and identify their points of entrance in the food production and processing chain.
Control Measures: As food authorities we recommend implementing control options to manage the risk caused by Bacillus cereus group organisms – including Bt- and their toxins. E.g. recommend to the food producer waiting times between Bt treatment and harvest as well as recommend to the consumers to keep foods refrigerated at ≤6°C and keep the storage temperature of heated food >52°C to control Bacillus cereus group strains in the food chain.
Whole Genome Sequencing: The application of whole genome sequencing is suggested to provide unambiguous identification of strains used as biopesticides and for their safety assessment. This approach aids in identifying markers for commercial B. thuringiensis strains and allows for precise identification of organisms involved in food-borne outbreaks.
Regulation and Guidelines: As food authority we focus on establishing regulations and guidelines for the use of Bacillus thuringiensis biopesticides, restricting the use to specific strains and ensuring that the products meet safety standards. We need to monitor proper application of Bt biopesticides, using the recommended doses and time intervals between application and harvest.
. General aim: The use of Bacillus thuringiensis biopesticides is a topic of concern for public health authorities due to the potential risks associated with these products. . Scientific foundation: Reconsider taxonomy-based risk assessment:  Bt strains display a similar repertoire of potential virulence genes on their chromosome as B. cereus sensu stricto strains, and these genes can be actively expressed in Bt strains. This questions the relevance of the separate species status of Bt. Since Bt cannot be distinguished from B. cereus with the classical methods currently used in food and clinical diagnostics, the levels of B. cereus that are considered a risk for consumers are also likely to be valid for Bt.
Integration of genetic and genomics in diagnostics: Whole genome sequencing should be applied to provide unambiguous identification of Bt strains used as biopesticides and enable detailed characterization of outbreak strains. Markers should be identified for high pathogenic B. cereus group strains and Bt biopesticide strains to allow regular monitoring and easy differentiation in suspected outbreak situations.
Sustainable and prudent use of Bt biopesticides: Field studies after application of Bt biopesticides are needed to establish pre-harvest intervals and monitor factors leading to transfer of Bacillus cereus group strains from the environment to foods.
. Ethical foundation: Human health: Bt strains possess the same genetic virulence determinants as B. cereus, which could provoke human illnesses. The levels of B. cereus that pose a risk to consumers are likely applicable to B. thuringiensis due to their genetic similarity.
Sustainability: B. thuringiensis biopesticides are considered environmentally friendly as they offer an alternative to synthetic chemical pesticides, reducing the environmental impact associated with traditional chemical insecticides. However, there are limited studies on the long-term effects of using Bacillus thuringiensis biopesticides on the environment and the impact of Bt biopesticides on biodiversity is controversially discussed.
Consumer:
Description: As a consumer, my primary concern is the safety, health, and well-being of my family and myself. I am also interested in the environmental impacts of agricultural practices, particularly in relation to the food we consume. I want to ensure that the food supply is free from harmful chemicals and that farming practices are sustainable, promoting both human and ecological health. Moreover, in my opinion transparent communication of food safety related risks as well as gapless knowledge transfer of methods and substances used in the global food supply chain are non-negotiable.. Short-term goals: •	Ensure that all food products available in the market are safe for consumption and free from harmful residues.
•	Obtain clear, transparent information about the methods and substances used in food production.
•	Advocate for clear labelling of food prudcts to inform consumers about the use of Bacillus thuringiensis in agriculture, allowing for informed choices.
•	Advocate for rigorous testing and regulation of biopesticides to prevent potential health risks.
•	Promote for independent research activities on potential adverse and long-term side effects of Bacillus thuringiensis used as biopesticide on human, animal, and environmental health (One Health approach)
•	Express interest in supporting research efforts to develop Bt strains with reduces risks and explore alterntave, integrated post management strategies 
. General aim: My general aim is to consume nutritious and healthy food and at the same time accepting agricultural practices that balance the need for pest control with the imperative of maintaining high standards of food safety and environmental protection. This includes promoting the responsible use of biopesticides like Bacillus thuringiensis, provided they are proven to be safe, effective, and environmentally friendly. This includes exploring alternative pest control methods for long-term sustainability.. Scientific foundation: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a naturally occurring soil bacterium that has been used as a biopesticide for many years. Scientific studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in controlling various pests while being relatively safe for humans and non-target species. Bt produces proteins that are toxic to specific insect larvae but are generally considered non-toxic to mammals, birds, and fish.
However, recent studies have raised some concerns about the safety and long-term impacts of Bt:
•	Resistance Development: There is evidence that pests can develop resistance to Bt, which could lead to the increased use of other, potentially more harmful pesticides.
•	Non-target Effects: Some studies suggest that Bt could have unintended effects on non-target organisms, including beneficial insects and soil microbiota .
•	Gene Transfer: There is ongoing debate about the potential for horizontal gene transfer between Bt crops and wild relatives, which could have ecological consequences .
•	Human Health: Although Bt is generally considered safe for humans, more comprehensive studies are needed to fully understand any long-term health effects, particularly with increased and prolonged exposure .
. Ethical foundation: From an ethical standpoint, the use of Bt aligns with the principles of reducing chemical pesticide usage, thus lowering the potential for harmful residues on food and in the environment. Ethically, it is imperative to protect consumer health and the ecosystem. The precautionary principle should guide the use of Bt, ensuring that any potential risks are thoroughly evaluated and managed.
Recent ethical concerns include:
•	Advocate for consumer access to safe and healthy food: Consumers have a right to access safe, healthy and nutritious food regardless their economic situtation, location or educational background.
•	Informed Consent, transparency and open communication: Consumers have a right to know how their food is produced and to make informed choices. Transparency about the use of Bt and its potential risks as well as mitigation strategies is essential.
•	Environmental Stewardship: Ethical farming practices should prioritize the protection of biodiversity and the health of ecosystems. This includes assessing and mitigating any potential negative impacts of Bt on non-target species and the environment.
•	Sustainability: Promoting sustainable agricultural practices that support long-term food security without compromising environmental health is crucial. The use of Bt should be part of a broader strategy that includes integrated pest management and other sustainable practices.
